newsitem.title: USA: Bill to allow tobacco suits in California defeated.
newsitem.headline: Bill to allow tobacco suits in California defeated.

text.p: California's Assembly defeated a bill on Thursday that would have made it easier for smokers in the state to sue tobacco companies.
Sen. Quentin Kopp's bill, which failed by five votes, would have made sweeping changes to a 1987 state law that gave tobacco companies immunity from product liability suits.
The changes proposed by Kopp, an independent, would have cleared the way for tobacco-related personal injury, wrongful death and other claims by individual smokers.
The bill was defeated after a lengthy debate. Opponents argued that smokers know the risks.
"I smoke. I'm fully aware of the health risks. Every smoker knows there's a risk involved," said Assemblyman Brett Granlund, a Republican.
A far more limited tobacco bill, by Assembly Speaker Cruz Bustamante, was approved by the legislature and signed by the governor earlier in June.
Bustamante's bill clarified existing state law, allowing the state and other public entities to sue the tobacco industry, but did not address the claims of individuals.
Kopp spokesman Randall Henry said the senator was "very disappointed" by his bill's failure.
"You could see tobacco industry lobbyists outside the floor of the Assembly, and they weren't there for their health or for any other reason than to defeat this bill," Henry said.

California sued the tobacco industry this month to recoup the costs of treating smoking-related illnesses. Last week, negotiators for states that had sued cigarette companies reached a proposed $368.5 billion settlement with the industry.
